articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Shipping Network, Issues New General Licenses and Removes Belarus, North Korea Entities
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has imposed new Iran-related designations, targeting five individuals, four companies, and nine vessels involved in an Iranian shadow fleet network. The designated entities include Panama-based law firm Karnakis and Karnakis, Roxette Maritime Shipping and Trading, Singapore-based Amigoz Singapore, and UAE-based Whales Shipping Line. These actions are part of Washington's 'Operation Economic Outcast' campaign, aimed at restricting Iranian financial and commercial networks supporting Tehran's military activities and other illicit operations.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued Iran General License GG, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving Karnakis and Karnakis, and Iran General License HH, permitting wind-down activities, limited safety and environmental transactions, and the offloading of cargo involving certain blocked persons or vessels. Additionally, OFAC issued Russia-related General License 131K, which authorizes certain transactions for the negotiation and entry into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH and related maintenance activities.

Furthermore, OFAC announced the removal of certain entities from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List under the Belarus and North Korea sanctions programs. These removals include Chinese national Lu Hezheng and two Chinese entities, Shanghai Moxing Cultural Media Co. Ltd. (also known as Moxing Cartoon) and Shanghai Hongman Cartoon and Animation Design Studio, previously sanctioned for ties to a North Korean government-run animation studio. Belarusian national Andrei Alekseevich Rybakov was also delisted from the Belarus sanctions program.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements PAIPA Designations, Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These designations are accompanied by the issuance of associated general licenses to mitigate any unintended consequences.

The PAIPA aims to combat intellectual property theft that harms American businesses and national security. Further details on the specific individuals or entities designated under this act were not immediately available in the initial announcement.

The issuance of general licenses alongside the designations suggests that OFAC is seeking to provide clear guidance and minimize disruption to legitimate trade and transactions while still enforcing the objectives of the PAIPA.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License for Earthquake Relief
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued Venezuela-related General License 60A, titled 'Authorizing Transactions Related to Earthquake Relief Efforts in Venezuela.' This amendment aims to facilitate humanitarian aid and recovery operations in the country following recent seismic activity.
In addition to the amended general license, OFAC also issued one amended Frequently Asked Question (FAQ 1263) to provide further clarity and guidance regarding the authorized transactions.
This action underscores OFAC's commitment to allowing humanitarian assistance to reach those in need, even within sanctioned jurisdictions, by providing specific authorizations for such efforts.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian and Cuban Entities, Issues New and Amended General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation, alongside the issuance of new and amended general licenses and frequently asked questions. This action is part of ongoing efforts to target illicit financial activities and support for sanctioned regimes.

The Iran-related designations are linked to 'Operation Economic Outcast,' which aims to disrupt Iranian international financial networks and shadow banking architecture, as well as the Iranian regime's abuse of religious charity networks. The specific entities designated were not detailed in the initial announcement but are expected to be involved in circumventing existing sanctions.

The Cuba designation targets the state-owned Banco Internacional de Comercio, S.A. (BICSA). The accompanying new and amended general licenses and FAQs are intended to provide guidance and clarify the scope of authorized transactions following these designations.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuelan Official Jorge Jesús Rodríguez Gómez from SDN List
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has removed Jorge Jesús Rodríguez Gómez, a prominent Venezuelan official, from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List. This action lifts asset-blocking restrictions and allows U.S. persons to engage in transactions with him that were previously prohibited.

Rodríguez Gómez, who serves as the President of Venezuela's National Assembly, was initially designated in 2018. His removal covers five separate entries associated with his name in OFAC's database, all linked to the same individual.

While OFAC did not provide a specific explanation for the decision, this removal is seen as a significant step in Washington's evolving sanctions policy toward Venezuela, signaling a potential shift towards diplomatic engagement and structured access to the country's resources.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities in Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Operations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations under its Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism sanctions programs. These actions target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and terrorist financing networks.

While specific details of the designated parties were not immediately available in the initial announcement, these designations are part of ongoing efforts to disrupt criminal enterprises that pose threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

Such designations typically result in the blocking of all property and interests in property of the designated persons that are within U.S. jurisdiction, and generally prohibit U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with them.

articles.headline: OFAC Settles with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, Designates International Criminal Court, and Removes Burma Entity
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarding firm. Pegasus agreed to remit $175,015 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of the Illicit Drug Trafficking Sanctions Regulations and the Reporting, Procedures and Penalties Regulations.

The apparent violations stemmed from Pegasus facilitating the importation of a machine supplied by a designated company and failing to fully respond to an OFAC subpoena for six months. OFAC determined that Pegasus's conduct was non-egregious and not voluntarily disclosed, but noted the company's extensive remedial measures.

In a separate action, OFAC designated the entire International Criminal Court (ICC) to its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List under Executive Order 14203. Concurrently, OFAC issued four general licenses (GL 13, 14, 15, and 16) authorizing certain transactions involving the ICC, including a 180-day wind-down period. Additionally, OFAC announced the removal of a Burma-related designation from its SDN List.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Russia-Related General License for Diesel Fuel Imports
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued Russia-related General License 135, titled 'Authorizing Transactions Related to the Sale, Delivery, Offloading, and Importation of Diesel Fuel of Russian Federation Origin.' This general license temporarily authorizes certain transactions involving Russian-origin diesel fuel until April 7, 2027.

This authorization comes amidst rising global diesel prices and follows an announcement by President Donald Trump regarding a deal with Russia to supply diesel to U.S. and global markets. The move, however, has faced scrutiny and legal uncertainty, as it appears to be at odds with broader U.S. efforts to target Russia's energy sector.

General License 135 authorizes all transactions otherwise prohibited by Russian harmful foreign activities sanctions or Ukraine-/Russia-related sanctions that are related to the sale, delivery, offloading, or importation of Russian-origin diesel fuel. However, it does not authorize debits to accounts of the Central Bank of the Russian Federation, the National Wealth Fund of the Russian Federation, or the Ministry of Finance at U.S. financial institutions.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Issues New General Licenses for Iran and Russia
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, further expanding sanctions against entities and individuals supporting the Iranian regime. These designations are part of ongoing efforts to counter Iran's destabilizing activities.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License, the specifics of which were not detailed in the initial announcement but are intended to provide carve-outs for certain transactions. Additionally, an amended Russia-related General License was issued, indicating adjustments to existing authorizations concerning transactions involving Russia.

These actions reflect the U.S. government's continued strategy of applying economic pressure on both Iran and Russia through targeted sanctions and the strategic use of general licenses to manage the impact on legitimate activities.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11.6 Million Over Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to settle its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of various OFAC sanctions programs. These programs targeted Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The apparent violations occurred when Bank of America processed payments involving blocked banks, failed to appropriately prioritize alerts for customers matching blocked persons, did not promptly update watchlists following OFAC designations, and mishandled business accounts associated with blocked persons due to human error.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were non-egregious but largely not voluntarily self-disclosed. This settlement is part of a larger enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury Department, totaling over $1.21 billion in penalties against Bank of America for anti-money laundering and sanctions law violations.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Pays $175,015 to Settle OFAC Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarding firm, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC's Illicit Drug Trafficking Sanctions Regulations and Reporting, Procedures and Penalties Regulations.

The violations involved Pegasus dealing in blocked property by facilitating the importation of a machine supplied by a designated company between September 2023 and February 2024. Additionally, Pegasus failed to respond fully to an OFAC subpoena for six months.

OFAC determined that the conduct was non-egregious and not voluntarily disclosed. The settlement amount reflects OFAC's consideration of general factors, including Pegasus's extensive remedial measures and enhanced reporting commitments.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $1.4 Million by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has been assessed a civil penalty of $1,427,230 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for sanctions violations. The details of the specific violations were not immediately released in the summary.

This substantial penalty underscores OFAC's commitment to enforcing U.S. sanctions laws against individuals who engage in prohibited transactions or activities. The enforcement action serves as a reminder of the personal liability associated with sanctions non-compliance.

OFAC regularly pursues enforcement actions against individuals and entities found to be in violation of the various sanctions programs it administers, highlighting the importance of due diligence and adherence to regulatory requirements.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $60,764
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. has reached a settlement with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to pay $60,764 for apparent violations of sanctions regulations. The specific nature of the violations was not detailed in the public summary.

This civil penalty highlights the importance for companies, regardless of their industry, to maintain robust sanctions compliance programs to prevent inadvertent dealings with sanctioned entities or jurisdictions.

OFAC's enforcement actions aim to promote adherence to U.S. foreign policy and national security goals by deterring prohibited transactions and encouraging effective compliance measures across all sectors.

articles.headline: Global Markets React to Mixed Economic Signals and Geopolitical Tensions
body: Global financial markets are exhibiting mixed reactions this week, influenced by a combination of economic data releases and persistent geopolitical tensions. Major indices in the U.S. and Europe saw modest gains, while Asian markets showed more varied performance. Investors are closely monitoring inflation figures and central bank commentary for clues on future monetary policy.

Energy prices, particularly for diesel, have been a significant factor, with recent U.S. actions to authorize imports of Russian diesel fuel drawing both support and criticism. This move aims to alleviate high domestic prices but raises questions about its alignment with broader sanctions against Russia.

The ongoing situation in Ukraine and the Middle East continues to contribute to market volatility, with investors seeking safe-haven assets amidst the uncertainty. Trade discussions and supply chain disruptions also remain key concerns for businesses worldwide.

articles.headline: Diesel Prices Remain Elevated Amidst Supply Concerns and Geopolitical Maneuvers
body: Global diesel prices continue to hover near record highs, creating significant pressure on transportation, logistics, and various industries. The elevated prices are attributed to a confluence of factors, including robust demand, limited refining capacity, and ongoing geopolitical instability impacting crude oil supplies.

Recent efforts by the U.S. to authorize the importation of Russian-origin diesel fuel, through OFAC General License 135, represent a strategic attempt to inject more supply into the market and temper price increases. This decision, however, has sparked debate regarding its potential impact on the effectiveness of sanctions against Russia.

Analysts are closely watching how these supply-side interventions, coupled with evolving geopolitical dynamics, will influence the trajectory of diesel prices in the coming months. The volatility in energy markets remains a key concern for economic stability worldwide.

articles.headline: OCC Releases October Enforcement Actions, Including Major Penalties for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has released its enforcement actions for October 2026, highlighting significant penalties against major financial institutions for deficiencies in their Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) compliance programs. These actions underscore the OCC's commitment to ensuring robust financial crime prevention measures within the banking sector.

Among the notable actions, American Express National Bank was issued a Cease and Desist Order and a civil money penalty of $350 million for BSA compliance program deficiencies, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and customer due diligence violations.

Bank of America, National Association, also faced a civil money penalty of $750 million for similar BSA compliance program deficiencies, including failures in suspicious activity reporting and inaccurate transmittor name information in wire transfers. These penalties reflect the OCC's focus on holding institutions accountable for maintaining effective AML frameworks.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: U.S. Sanctions Target Iran's Shadow Fleet and Financial Networks
body: The United States has intensified its economic pressure on Iran with new sanctions targeting a sophisticated shadow fleet network and associated financial infrastructure. These measures, announced by the U.S. Treasury Department, aim to disrupt Iran's ability to circumvent existing sanctions and fund its illicit activities.

The sanctions specifically target five individuals, four companies, and nine vessels, including a Panama-based law firm and shipping businesses linked to Singapore and the United Arab Emirates. This action is part of Washington's 'Operation Economic Outcast' campaign, which seeks to restrict Iranian financial and commercial networks supporting Tehran's military and cyber operations.

The U.S. government asserts that these networks are crucial for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and its various illicit endeavors. Under U.S. sanctions rules, assets belonging to designated individuals and entities within American jurisdiction are blocked, and U.S. persons are generally prohibited from conducting transactions with them.

articles.headline: U.S. Imposes Sweeping Sanctions on International Criminal Court, Drawing Condemnation
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has imposed institution-wide sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), adding the entire court to its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List. This unprecedented move, enacted under Executive Order 14203, aims to disrupt the ICC's assets and its capacity to operate.

The sanctions are intended to 'defend US sovereignty and neutralize the threat posed by the ICC,' according to the U.S. Department of State. This action follows previous U.S. sanctions targeting individuals associated with the ICC, including judges and prosecutors, but marks a significant escalation by targeting the institution itself.

The decision has drawn strong condemnation from the ICC, which rejected the measure, and from the UN Secretary-General, who warned of an impact on the court's work. The EU High Representative also expressed deep regret and urged the U.S. to reverse the measures. OFAC concurrently issued four general licenses to authorize certain transactions and a 180-day wind-down period for operations involving the court.

articles.headline: OCC Issues Cease and Desist Order and $350 Million Penalty to American Express National Bank for BSA Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has issued a Cease and Desist Order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah. The enforcement action addresses significant deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program.

The OCC found that American Express National Bank failed to timely file suspicious activity reports (SARs) and exhibited violations in its customer due diligence and customer identification programs. These failures indicate a systemic breakdown in the bank's anti-money laundering controls.

The substantial penalty and cease and desist order underscore the OCC's stringent approach to enforcing BSA/AML regulations and its expectation for financial institutions to maintain robust compliance frameworks to prevent illicit financial activities.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Fines Bank of America $750 Million for BSA/AML Program Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has assessed a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, National Association, Charlotte, North Carolina. This penalty is a result of widespread deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program.

The OCC identified failures in Bank of America's ability to timely file suspicious activity reports (SARs) and issues with sending wires that contained inaccurate transmittor name information. These shortcomings highlight significant weaknesses in the bank's anti-money laundering (AML) controls.

This enforcement action is part of a broader set of penalties announced by the U.S. Treasury Department against Bank of America, totaling over $1.21 billion for violations of anti-money laundering and sanctions laws. The OCC's penalty is the largest in its history.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Issues Prohibition Orders Against Bank Employees for Embezzlement
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has issued prohibition orders against two institution-affiliated parties (IAPs) for embezzlement. These actions reinforce the accountability of individuals for their conduct within the banking system.
Jennifer Hamblin, a Vault Teller at a Cincinnati, Ohio, branch of Fifth Third Bank, N.A., was issued a prohibition order for embezzling approximately $292,000 in customer funds.

Similarly, Christopher Organista, a Former Operations Processor at the La Mirada, California Operations Center of U.S. Bank National Association, Cincinnati, Ohio, received a prohibition order for embezzling approximately $194,131 in bank customer funds. These orders prohibit the individuals from any further participation in the affairs of a bank or other financial institution.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Report on Debanking Practices Signals Potential Regulatory Changes
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has released its long-awaited report, 'Guaranteeing Fair Banking for All Americans,' detailing findings from its supervisory review of 'debanking' practices at the nine largest national banks. The report concludes that these banks maintained policies or practices that may have influenced the denial or limitation of financial services based on customers' political or religious beliefs or lawful business activities.

While the report did not announce any immediate enforcement actions or penalties, Comptroller Jonathan Gould indicated that the OCC is 'not confident' that the banks' current remedial efforts will be sufficient. The OCC is now considering further changes to the regulatory and supervisory framework applicable to large banks.

The OCC is also exploring actions to prevent banks from discriminating based on political or religious beliefs and to address the role of reputation risk in bank decision-making. This signals a new phase in the federal debanking campaign, moving beyond policy statements to potential concrete supervisory and enforcement consequences.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
